newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Progress made over NATO in Albright talks - Russia.
newsitem.headline: Progress made over NATO in Albright talks - Russia.

text.p: Russia said on Friday "certain progress" was made in talks over a NATO-Russia security charter during a visit to Moscow by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

A statement by the chief Foreign Ministry spokesman, Gennady Tarasov, gave no details but said: "Certain progress has emerged in the discussion of issues related to the preparation of the document setting up relations between Russia and NATO".
Albright and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov held a second, unscheduled round of talks on Friday aimed at trying to narrow differences over NATO's planned eastward expansion.

Neither made any comment after the meeting, which delayed Albright's departure from Moscow. The two were trying to shape a NATO-Russia security charter designed to calm Russian fears over the alliance's enlargement to include former East Bloc states.
Tarasov said Primakov had briefed President Boris Yeltsin, who spoke to Albright by telephone on Thursday, over the results of the second round of negotiations.
Albright and Primakov met for two hours on Thursday and said later they had made progress but that tough issues remained to be resolved if a May 27 target date for signing the charter was to be met.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, who leads the talks for the alliance, is to see Primakov in Luxembourg on May 6.
Western officials say the charter would set up a joint council with the Russians which would give Moscow a voice in key decisions affecting its security interests in Europe.
But Russia is demanding binding guarantees from NATO that it will not move nuclear arms or conventional forces into the territory of new members.
NATO says it has no plans to do so, but is reluctant to be tied down legally.

Also holding up the charter negotiations is the failure so far of 30-nation Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) talks in Vienna to agree on new force levels on Russia's borders in the new post-Cold War era.
